description:
#### What type of PR is this?
/kind bug

#### What this PR does / why we need it:

This PR changes the behavior of the scheduler when it preempts the pods that are in "WaitOnPermit" phase. Currently the pods are Rejected by a preemption plugin which moves the victim pod to unschedulable queue, adding the information about preemption to PodCondition. It means that this pod will be stuck in unschedulable queue until some event in the cluster pushes it back to backoff/active queue. It seems undesirable as it does not give a strong signal to the component owning the pod to recreate it (compared to default preemption which deletes the pod completely). After this PR the victim pod will be moved to the backoff queue, allowing the scheduler to try to schedule it once again after some time. 

#### Which issue(s) this PR is related to:

This was found as a part of the https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/132332

#### Special notes for your reviewer:

#### Does this PR introduce a user-facing change?

```release-note
Changed the behavior of default scheduler preemption plugin when preempting pods that are in "WaitOnPermit" phase. They are now moved to the scheduler backoff queue instead of being marked as unschedulable. 
```

#### Additional documentation e.g., KEPs (Kubernetes Enhancement Proposals), usage docs, etc.:

N/A

/sig scheduling

nit:
```suggestion
		return fwk.NewStatus(fwk.Wait, "waiting"), time.Minute
```
Won't this waiting step be fulfilled even without the preemption? Maybe it's just worth to verify that at the end both pods are scheduled - preemptor on node1 and victim on node2.
Done.

I believe it's not the case, the first attempt should fail after one minute of waiting on permit and here we wait only 15s so it should not be possible that the pod fails on timeout and then is rescheduled. The WaitOnPermit has to be cancelled by preemption. However the second part of the comment is valid and I added a validation of the state of 2 pods at the end.

When between calling `ev.Handler.GetWaitingPod` and `waitingPod.Preempt` the pod has ended waiting on permit, the preemption won't take any effect and the preemptor can be stuck as unschedulable. In #135502 you added handling similar case to the `GetPodInPrebind` rejection. Maybe you could add such for waiting pods as well?

Technically it's waiting for the victim to be scheduled, not the preemptor.

This also leaves room for breaking this test in a flaky way, e.g. the scheduling logic may for some reason schedule the victim first, and the test may not see the preemptor as scheduled yet, as it didn't wait for it.

Have you considered waiting for both the victim and the preemptor to be scheduled?

In the lines 1794-1800 we verify that the preemptor is scheduled on big node.

Changed comment to better reflect the logic.

Right, but we don't wait for the preemptor to be scheduled, we only check its state once the victim is scheduled. So if something breaks the assumption that once the victim is scheduled, the preemptor is also scheduled, the test may become flaky instead of consistently failing / passing. This is because the scheduler loop runs in parallel to the test code.
Good idea, applied.
Yes, you are right, changed it to explicitly wait for the victim in a separate loop.

I'm not sure if this will work as expected. `w.s` is a buffered channel. If the pod is allowed/rejected by some plugin, WaitOnPermit func consumes that message and then Preempt can enqueue the next one and return true (when it should return false). Probably we need an additional field to say whether the Allow/Reject/Permit was called or not.

You are right I did not notice that this is a buffered channel. The comments in Allow/Reject above the select clauses are implying that this is a non buffered channel that will run a default case if there is no receiver. 

Created a separate variable for that and updated comments to reflect what is really going on
